title: ICE Makes Arrests at NYC Immigration Courts Despite Federal Judge's Ban
excerpt: At least five people were detained inside Manhattan courthouses in recent weeks. ICE claims criminal histories justify the arrests, but advocates say the agency is flouting judicial orders.
body:
• ICE arrested at least five people inside New York City immigration courts in recent weeks, despite two federal court orders banning most such arrests.
  • ICE is citing the criminal histories of those targeted and claiming courthouses are the "safest location" for arrests in "sanctuary cities" like New York.
  • Immigrant advocacy groups have asked the federal judge overseeing the case to intervene, saying at least one arrest involved a man whose only criminal record was a trespassing charge from his initial entry.
  • The arrests create a chilling effect for all immigrants with court hearings — including Indian nationals in removal proceedings — who must choose between attending their hearing and risking detention.

Arrests Resume Despite Judicial Orders

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested at least five people inside New York City immigration courts in recent weeks, despite two federal court orders banning the practice in most cases, according to The City Reporter.

https://x.com/HeltLawGroup/status/2078576936805154844

The arrests occurred at the Manhattan immigration courts at 26 Federal Plaza and 290 Broadway, two of the three courthouses covered by a May 18 ruling from U.S. District Judge P. Kevin Castel. That ruling largely prohibited ICE from conducting civil immigration enforcement actions in or near the courts, reverting to Biden-era 2021 guidance that allowed courthouse arrests only in rare cases involving threats to national security or public safety.

A federal judge in California issued a similar ruling in late June that barred most courthouse arrests nationwide.

ICE's New Justification

In court filings this week, ICE laid out a new rationale for the arrests: the criminal histories of those targeted and the claim that New York's sanctuary city policies make alternative arrest locations unsafe.

"At-large arrests in sanctuary cities like New York tend to trigger protests and intervention by agitators and bystanders, making alternative locations in New York unsafe and the safest location for the arrests."

— Roberto Rodriguez, Acting Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer, ICE

ICE said its officers query arrest databases and compile lists of targets ahead of their immigration court hearings. A spokesperson said one of the men arrested had a trespassing conviction, another had assault and criminal obstruction of breathing charges, and a third faced pending attempted murder charges. ICE did not immediately comment on the fourth and fifth arrests.

Advocates Push Back

Attorney Katherine Rosenfeld, representing African Communities Together and other immigrant groups in the ongoing litigation, asked Judge Castel to intervene. In a June 29 letter, she highlighted the case of a man whose sole criminal history was a trespassing charge related to his initial entry into the United States in 2024.

"Since then, he has complied with immigration supervision; appeared for immigration-court hearings at least three times; and had no contact with the criminal system," Rosenfeld wrote. She argued his arrest "appears to flout" the court's order, noting that "the government cannot reasonably contend that an individual whose sole criminal history stems from a charge arising from his entry into the United States poses a threat to public safety."

Two of the arrests, which occurred on June 25, were captured on video by photographer Christina Panagi. Attorneys from Make the Road New York filed suit on both men's behalf seeking their release.

The Chilling Effect on Immigrant Communities

The arrests create an impossible calculation for immigrants scheduled to appear in court: attend the hearing and risk being detained by ICE, or skip the hearing and face an automatic deportation order issued in absentia. The ACLU's Amy Belsher called the May 18 ruling "an enormous win," noting that for months prior, "masked ICE officers ambush noncitizens in courthouse hallways, throw immigrant New Yorkers to the ground, and tear children from their parents."

For Indian nationals in removal or adjustment proceedings — a population that has grown as visa overstays and asylum claims increase — the courthouse arrest policy adds another layer of risk to an already stressful legal process. Immigration attorneys have reported that clients are increasingly reluctant to appear for hearings, even when they have strong cases.

What Happens Next

Judge Castel has not yet ruled on the advocates' request to enforce his earlier order. The back-and-forth comes as the Trump administration faces broader scrutiny over its immigration enforcement tactics. A UN panel this week expressed concern that the White House was transforming the immigration court system "from a forum for independent, individualized adjudication into an instrument for implementing deportation objectives," according to Reuters. More than 100 immigration judges out of approximately 700 have been fired or pushed out since Trump returned to office in January 2025.
